vignette:
She is twenty-one years old, but when she speaks, her voice carries a weight that belongs to someone much older. She came to therapy because her partner said she was "disappearing" - that sometimes she would be sitting right next to him on the couch, but her eyes would go somewhere else, somewhere dark, and she wouldn't hear his voice until he touched her arm. She agreed to come, she told me, because she is tired of being afraid of her own bedroom.

She grew up on a small island in Oceania, surrounded by ocean and family. She wanted to help people, so she trained as a nurse. When she turned nineteen, she joined a peacekeeping mission in a conflict zone, deployed with a medical unit. She was proud. She believed in the work.

The traumatic event happened on a Tuesday. She remembers the heat first - thick, wet, pressing against her skin. Her team had been called to a village after reports of an ambush. She was the one who triaged the wounded. There was a young girl, maybe seven or eight, with shrapnel wounds across her chest and face. The girl was conscious, and she kept reaching for her mother, who was already dead a few meters away. The patient's name was Talia. She never forgot that name.

She worked on Talia for nearly an hour. The surgical field was inadequate; the lighting flickered from a generator. She held pressure, she packed wounds, she tried to keep her talking. At one point, Talia looked up and said, "It hurts," and then she stopped breathing. No dramatic explosion. No heroic last words. Just silence and the sound of flies. The body grew still, and she remembers feeling her own pulse in her teeth.

She was rotated out two weeks later. She did not tell anyone what happened. She told herself she was fine. She came home and resumed nursing at a busy urban hospital, working the emergency department. At first, she thought the shift was good - she could stay busy, stay focused. But now, every time a pediatric trauma case comes in, she smells the generator. She hears the flies. She has to excuse herself to the staff bathroom and press her forehead against the cool tile until her heart slows down.

Her partner is kind, patient. But she cannot be intimate with him anymore. Not because she doesn't love him, but because the sound of his breathing at night reminds her of someone trying to stay quiet before an attack. She sleeps in the living room most nights, curled on the couch with the television on low, because the dark is a threat. She avoids war movies, news about conflict zones, even the word "deployment." She stopped answering calls from her old unit. She deleted the photo of Talia from her phone, but she still sees her face when she closes her eyes.

At work last week, a child came in with a laceration from a fall. The mother was crying. She found herself unable to approach the bedside. Her hands started trembling, and she felt a hot wave of nausea. She told the charge nurse she had a stomach bug and went home early. She spent the rest of the day lying on the bathroom floor at home, listening to her own breath, convinced that something terrible was about to happen.

She does not want to talk about the military. She does not want to remember the deployment. But the deployment remembers her. It shows up in the way she scans every room for exits, in the way she flinches when a car backfires, in the way she has stopped making plans for the future because she is not sure she will be alive to see them.

She has not slept more than four hours in a row in eight months. She has not cried since it happened. She wants to feel something, but all she feels is the cold, flat hum of vigilance. She told me, "I am still nursing. I am still here. But I am not in my body anymore. I am somewhere else, and I don't know how to come back."
